segments.text: Triggers: code that runs by itself when data changes.
A trigger is a block of PL SQL that Oracle runs automatically. Nobody calls it: like a motion-sensor light, the event switches it on.
Each trigger has an event: an insert, update or delete on a table. A timing: before or after the change. And a level: once per statement, or once for each row.
First, a BEFORE trigger at row level. It fires before each row is stored, and it sees the new value as colon NEW dot grade.
Try to set a grade of eleven. The trigger raises an application error, and the update is rejected.
Set seven point four six instead. It passes the check, and the trigger rounds it to one decimal, so seven point five is stored.
Now an AFTER trigger. It fires once the row has changed, so it is the place for an audit trail.
For each updated row, it inserts a line into grade audit, with the old grade from colon OLD and the new grade from colon NEW.
Raise every Databases grade by half a point: three rows change, so three audit lines appear.
The WHEN clause skips rows whose grade does not really change. Setting Ana's grade to nine again writes nothing.
A row trigger sees two versions of the row. Colon OLD holds the values before the change, and colon NEW the values after it.
An update has both. An insert has no old row, so colon OLD is null. A delete has no new row, so colon NEW is null.
Inside WHEN, write them without the colon.
Without FOR EACH ROW, a trigger is statement level. Grade notice fires once per update, however many rows it changes.
So one update that touches three Databases enrolments fires a statement trigger once, and a row trigger three times.
The order is fixed. BEFORE statement first. Then, for every row: BEFORE row, the change itself, and AFTER row. AFTER statement comes last.
Two warnings. A row trigger cannot query the table it is changing: Oracle stops with O R A zero four zero nine one, table is mutating.
And triggers are invisible. Another developer runs an update and wonders where the extra changes came from.
Keep them small. If a check constraint can do the job, use the constraint.
Practise it in the SQL section of the course site.
